Guettel’s lyrics, which focus attention on the intense interactions of Joe and Kirsten, could not be more potently rendered than by Brian d’Arcy James and Kelli O’Hara, two of New York’s foremost stage presences.
Above all, and despite the show's flaws, the score and James and O'Hara's singing guarantee a most memorable evening.
Days of Wine and Roses is a precipitous ski run of addiction and misery, and its raw display of both reverberated among the audience this critic sat among.
But on stage, Days of Wine and Roses ends up easier to respect for its ambition, and O’Hara and Brian d’Arcy James's stellar work, than to wholeheartedly recommend.

And although both performers are technically a bit too old for their roles, their powerful performances and obvious rapport make you feel deeply for their characters.

As a ruthless account of the fate that wrecks the lives of decent people, this is a grim, graphic, and demanding play, but as a musical, I watched them suffer but just wasn’t able to suffer with them the same way.
While Days of Wine and Roses is an ambitious and formidable attempt to musicalize this cautionary tale, ultimately it does not solve the problems inherent in the material.

Right now, the only major criticism to level at “Days of Wine and Roses” is that it took Guettel so long to write his third musical, which can easily take its place as one of the few great musicals of this century.

Director Michael Greif does fine work with his stars, who are unfailingly thoughtful throughout, but he can't keep Days of Wine and Roses from feeling predictable, a case history with a predestined conclusion.
Regardless of the shortcomings, the impact is distressing, and the outcome is devastating, ensuring this is not your typical evening of musical theater.
This is a master class in every way.

The shapes and forms of each unpacked the difficulty of engagement and love, but each spread was overflowing, sometimes with fine flavors and compelling narratives, but also with complexities that never found their footing...
The cumulative effects are impressive, but in the end, Days of Wine and Roses is more intellectually stimulating than intoxicatingly soul-stirring.
So it hurts to say this, but I found Days of Wine and Roses cruelly disappointing.
While it works well as a cautionary tale about the dangers of addiction and the epidemic of alcoholism in America, Days of Wine and Roses isn't quite as effective as a piece of musical theatre.
But this is an off-putting exercise on both a narrative and a musical level — one that may leaving you pining for less wine and many more roses.

cn.t: O'Hara and d'Arcy James deliver powerhouse performances in Guettel's operatic addiction musical, though critics split on whether this dark material should have been musicalized at all.
